Most small businesses have something in common: they are run by reluctant operators. These are owners who set out to provide a service to their local community, and ended up running a business instead. They did not sign up to become finance people, HR people, recruiters, billers, or claims specialists. They became those things because someone had to.

Dental practices are a perfect example. Dentists go to school to practice dentistry and care for patients. Instead many are stuck doing paperwork, hiring people, training and retaining staff, negotiating insurance contracts, fighting claims, and managing cash flow.

Across roughly 160,000 dental practices in the U.S., this work is increasingly hard to staff and expensive to get wrong. AI can already do much of this work today. It is just not in the hands of these businesses yet.

We think businesses will soon run themselves, and small businesses will be among the first. Today, we are thrilled to announce that a16z is leading Lassie’s $35 million Series A – and partnering with a team solving exactly this problem.

Lassie is building AI that runs small businesses, starting with dental practices. Co-founders Steijn Pelle and Frédéric Renken did not find this problem from a distance. After working in consumer fintech at Robinhood and Coinbase, Steijn learned from his own dentist, Dr. Kwon, how complex the financial administration of an SMB dental practice can be. He and Frédéric, who had built product at Superhuman and Uber, then worked inside Dr. Kwon’s office, processing payments by hand to understand the workflow from the inside.

This story is emblematic of how Steijn and Frédéric have approached building Lassie. Before writing a single line of code, they spent months talking to dentists, primary care doctors, and healthcare finance teams. Then they spent years building the infrastructure and integrations required for agents to operate directly within a practice’s workflow: reading insurance claims, reconciling payments, posting to the ledger, and flagging claims that need action. Lassie is not a copilot that creates more work for the practice to review. It does the work.

Lassie already works with more than 700 practices across 49 states, generates more than $10 million in annualized revenue, and provides practices with 250,000 hours of labor a year. Growth has come largely through referrals and inbound demand – a sign that customers are not just buying the product, but telling other practice owners about it. The most important benefit, customers say, is not simply doing the work faster. It is catching the underpayments, denials, and missing claims that used to slip through.

Dental is a strong first market because the pain is acute and the workflows are structured, repetitive, and high-value. But the larger insight is not dental-specific. Every small business is still held together by human labor: people answer phones, schedule work, hire and train staff, chase paperwork, collect payments, reconcile accounts, follow up on exceptions, and keep the business moving. The last generation of software gave businesses better tools. AI agents change the unit of value from software to labor. Lassie is starting with dental, but the broader opportunity is much larger: the small business that runs itself.

That is also why Lassie is difficult to replicate with a generic model alone. Running a small business is not one task; it is thousands of recurring workflows across customers, vendors, payments, forms, systems, and exceptions. The product has to understand the business, connect to the tools where work happens, know when to act, and know when to ask. Over time, the product learns from every completed workflow, building a knowledge layer that is difficult to recreate from scratch.

We are thrilled to partner with Steijn, Frédéric, and the Lassie team as they build toward one of the most important shifts in software: from tools that help businesses operate to agents that do the work. Lassie Raises $35M Led by Andreessen Horowitz to Build AI for Small Businesses to Run Themselves

Founded by early Robinhood and Superhuman product managers, Lassie is working on autonomous systems that handle the busywork

Currently operating in 700+ small businesses across 49 states, providing business owners with over 250,000 hours of labor each year

Lassie, the company building autonomous systems to run small businesses, announced it has raised $35 million in Series A financing, bringing its total capital raised to $47 million. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) with support from Night Capital, Rahul Vohra, founder and former CEO of Superhuman; Zach Perret, co-founder and CEO of Plaid; Taavet Hinrikus, co-founder and former CEO of Wise; Gokul Rajaram; and Brian Balfour, co-founder and CEO of Reforge.

AI can do a lot today. It writes software, passes bar exams, and generates realistic videos from simple prompts. But it can do so much more. It can help millions of small business owners by handling their busywork. Up until now, software has not removed this painstaking administrative work and has merely rearranged it. For the first time, software can interpret messy context, move across the endless systems that small businesses have, and do that work for an owner.

Nowhere is this more apparent than in doctors’ offices, the largest type of small businesses behind retail and food and beverage. A typical practice loses 100+ hours a month to administrative work and spends roughly $200,000 a year on staff that owners can barely find, let alone keep.

Today, Lassie’s agent goes into a practice's insurance portals, pulls reimbursements, reconciles them against records, updates the system-of-record, and verifies the funds in the bank. Operating in more than 700 practices across 49 states, Lassie currently provides businesses owners with over 250,000 hours of labor each year.

"Small business owners should be freed up from doing busywork, so they can focus on what they are passionate about," said Steijn Pelle, CEO and co-founder of Lassie. "After watching 700 businesses rely on Lassie to do a big part of their administration, I am convinced that the future is bright. They now use the time we save them to grow the business and spend more time with customers. And we are just getting started!”

“I am thrilled to partner with Steijn, Frédéric, and the team as they build towards one of the most important shifts in software: from tools that help businesses operate to agents that do the work,” said Alex Rampell, co-founder of Affirm and General Partner at a16z. “We think businesses will soon run themselves and Lassie is the perfect example that this is not a pipe dream. They are already making this a reality, providing many businesses with tens of hours of labor each month, and allowing business owners to focus on what they love doing, not busywork.”

“Before Lassie, I was drowning in paperwork where insurance companies would send me payments and I’d have to spend hours after seeing patients to manually enter hundreds of patients and thousands of procedure codes,” said Dr. Eric Kwon, founder of Grace Dental. “Now, Lassie saves us over 100 hours a month and payments that used to take four to five weeks hit our account in less than a week. Most importantly, Lassie has given me time back to focus on my patients, grow my practice, and spend time with my family.”

To accelerate Lassie’s growth and adoption, the company announced Alex Rampell, co-founder of Affirm and general partner of Andreessen Horowitz, will be joining Lassie’s Board of Directors. In addition, Dr. Ed Zuckerberg and Jason Warnick, former chief financial officer of Robinhood, will be joining the company as advisors.

To learn more about Lassie visit lassie.ai.

About Lassie

Lassie helps small businesses run themselves. By pushing the boundaries of autonomous systems, it handles the busywork for business owners. First, doctor’s offices.

Lassie was founded by Steijn Pelle, an early product manager at Robinhood and Coinbase, and Frédéric Renken, the first product hire of Superhuman. It is backed by Andreessen Horowitz, SV Angel, Homebrew, Go Global Ventures, Night Capital, and more. The company currently serves 700+ small businesses, providing owners with over 250,000 hours of labor each year.

Your recall list is three months behind, insurance verifications are piling up, and the idea of hiring help without adding another body to the break room sounds perfect until you start digging into what "dental virtual assistant" actually means in 2026.

Some listings talk about dental virtual assistant jobs remote with humans overseas doing billing, others describe virtual dentist jobs or virtual dental assistant jobs that are really just AI bots picking up the phone, and the salary ranges for dental VA jobs salary, dental virtual assistant salary, va dental assistant salary, and hello rache dental virtual assistant salary are so wide you can't tell if you're comparing apples to apples. ## What Is a Dental Virtual Assistant?

A dental virtual assistant is a human remote worker who handles administrative work for a practice without sitting in the office. The term gets stretched to cover AI tools too, but that conflation creates real confusion when you're trying to decide what to hire or buy.

Human VAs, often based in the Philippines or Latin America, log into your practice management system to schedule appointments, verify insurance, post payments, and chase claims. They are people doing a job remotely, not software.

AI receptionists and AI RCM tools are two separate categories that get lumped in under the same umbrella. AI receptionists answer phones, book appointments, and send reminders without a person in the loop: patient-facing work with its own complexity and risk. AI RCM tools handle back-office insurance posting: retrieving EOBs, reading line items, and writing payments into the PMS. These categories have different risk profiles, different use cases, and nothing to do with dental VA jobs.

## Dental Virtual Assistant Roles and Responsibilities

Dental VAs typically split their work into four buckets, with overlap depending on practice size and staffing gaps.

- Insurance coordination: verifying eligibility, breaking down patient benefits, submitting claims, and following up on aging or denied claims.
- Back office billing: posting EOBs into Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental, matching payments against deposits, and generating patient statements.
- Patient communication: sending reminders, answering billing questions, coordinating treatment financing, and chasing no-shows.
- Records management: updating charts, attaching X-rays to claims, and keeping documentation audit-ready.

## Dental Virtual Assistant Salary and Job Market Outlook

Pay scales depend heavily on whether you hire domestically or offshore, and the gap is wide.

US-based virtual dental assistants earn an average of $24.40 per hour, according to ZipRecruiter, with treatment coordinators and insurance specialists earning higher rates. Direct hires from the Philippines or Latin America run$1,200 to $2,000 per month fully loaded, often under a quarter of a stateside front desk hire.

Remote VA listings, including no-experience roles, have grown sharply on Indeed, OnlineJobs.ph, and agencies like MedVa, Hello Rache, and Wisdom Dental Billing. California, Texas, and Florida lead hiring.

## Human Virtual Assistants vs AI Dental Receptionists

These are three distinct categories, not two. Human VAs are remote labor with a login. AI receptionists are software that handles patient-facing work: picking up the phone, booking the slot, sending the reminder. AI RCM tools are a third bucket: back-office software that retrieves EOBs, maps CDT codes, and posts payments into your PMS with no human in the loop.

Patient-facing automation carries more risk: edge cases, complex conversations, and patient trust are harder for software to handle without gaps. Back-office automation is the opposite: structured data, rule-based logic, no patient interaction, and clear right-or-wrong outcomes make it prime for full automation. AI RCM runs faster than a human VA, is more secure (no person touching deposit data), more accurate (no manual entry errors), and usually cheaper once you factor in training, QA, and the cost of posting mistakes.

HIPAA does not ban offshore or remote help, but it puts the burden on you to protect PHI when a third party touches it. The California Dental Association urges practices to proceed carefully before granting outside access.

- Signed Business Associate Agreement with every VA, agency, or AI vendor handling patient data, covering breach notification and subcontractor terms.
- Encrypted channels for PHI: no SMS, no personal Gmail, no unsecured file shares. VPN access, audit logs, and role-based permissions are table stakes.
- Documented HIPAA training with annual refreshers, proof of completion stored alongside the BAA.

Offshore hires add a wrinkle. US enforcement against foreign workers is limited, so contract terms and technical controls carry most of the weight.

In-house admin staff costs more than salary. Front desk, billing, and office manager roles typically run 5 to 8 percent of collections, and total labor averages 27 percent of overhead per Dental CPAs once you fold in payroll taxes, premiums, PTO, and workspace.

Shopping for dental practice management software means reading the same feature checklist six times over. Patient scheduling, treatment planning, claims submission, everyone has it. Dentrix and Eaglesoft for mature all-in-one setups, Open Dental for customization, Curve and Denticon for cloud-native architecture, and Lassie for the insurance automation none of them include.

- Cloud options like Curve and Denticon remove server management but vary by practice size and fit
- Lassie automates EOB posting and bank reconciliation for practices on Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental

## What is Dental Practice Management Software?

Dental practice management software (PMS) is the system of record a dental office runs on. It holds patient charts, schedules, treatment plans, imaging, insurance claims, and ledgers in one place, so the front desk, hygienists, and dentists work from the same data. According to Grand View Research, the dental PMS market is projected to grow from $3.3 billion in 2026 to $6.8 billion by 2033, driven by the adoption of automation.

Clinically, a PMS stores radiographs, periodontal charts, and treatment notes. Administratively, it handles scheduling, eligibility checks, claim submission, payment posting, and patient billing. If a workflow touches a patient or a payer, it usually lives inside the PMS.

## How We Ranked Dental Practice Management Software

We weighed five PMS platforms (Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Curve, and Denticon) against the criteria that move the needle for dental practices in 2026. Lassie is covered separately as an insurance automation add-on that works alongside any of these systems, not as a PMS itself:

- Integration ecosystem. The most important factor. A PMS that opens cleanly to voice AI receptionists, insurance verification, AI charting, and recall tools lets you build the stack you want. Automated insurance verification eliminates hours of work and reduces claim denials substantially.
- Automation depth. How much of EOB posting, claims, and reconciliation runs without a human touching it.
- Architecture. Cloud vs. on-premises servers: what that means for uptime, updates, and IT overhead.
- Data ownership. Whether you can pull your records out in a usable format if you leave.
- Multi-location support. Shared tax IDs, separate ledgers, centralized reporting.
- Implementation lift. Onboarding time, training burden, and schedule disruption.

## Best Insurance Back-Office Automation for Dental Practices: Lassie

Lassie tackles the part of running a dental practice that every PMS leaves on staff: insurance payment posting and reconciliation. We read EOBs, post them into your PMS, and match against bank deposits with no manual keying.

### What Lassie does well

- Real-time EOB posting with custom rules for adjustments, write-offs, and downgrades
- Bank reconciliation to the cent, flagging overpayments and discrepancies
- Multi-location support across shared or separate tax IDs with location-level ledger routing
- Free EFT enrollment to kill paper checks and virtual credit card fees
- Automated secondary claim filing for Open Dental practices on Dental Exchange
- Cancel-anytime contracts, unlimited training, and direct account manager access
- Automated patient billing with statement generation, SMS delivery, and real-time flagging of unpaid balances after 30 days

### Where Lassie fits

Lassie works alongside your existing PMS, it does not replace it. You keep Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental for scheduling, charting, and clinical workflows; Lassie handles the insurance payment posting and reconciliation those systems leave to staff. Practices that file at least 70 percent of payments through commercial PPOs get the most value. Denticon users and practices with heavy Medicaid volume through Skygen-style administrators are not a fit yet.

### Trade-offs to know

Claim submission and aging follow-up stay with the staff. Automated appeals generation is now available in beta. Setup is $3,000 per location, and groups under a shared TIN must onboard every location at once.

Based on Lassie's customer case studies, practices report 4 to 7 percent more revenue after going live, against an ongoing 2 percent posting fee.

## Dentrix

Dentrix has anchored dental practice management for 30+ years and, according to the company, runs in 35,000+ US practices.

### What they offer

- All-in-one system tying scheduling, imaging, billing, analytics, and patient engagement
- Ascend automation for insurance eligibility and claims processing
- Real-time dashboards and smart reports for single or multi-location groups
- Built-in AI diagnostic tools for caries identification and treatment planning

Good for: Existing practices with Patterson Dental relationships wanting a mature, feature-rich system.

Limitation: Local installs need remote access, updates, and IT support that cloud-native options skip.

## Eaglesoft

According to Patterson Dental, Eaglesoft is used in nearly 30,000 practices and integrates with 55+ authorized software solutions.

### What they offer

- Deep digital imaging integration covering video, intraoral, and digital X-rays in a single patient record
- Open ecosystem for connecting third-party tools to customize workflows
- Eaglesoft Service Club with unlimited US-based support, free upgrades, and Schick warranty coverage
- HIPAA-compliant forms and processes baked in

Good for: Practices already invested in Patterson hardware and imaging equipment that want a single vendor for supplies and software.

Limitation: The interface looks like an older Windows app, and the learning curve is steep for new staff.

## Open Dental

Open Dental is highly customizable dental practice management software priced for clinics of any size. Its open-source foundation gives practices full data ownership and customization depth that proprietary systems can't match.

### What they offer

- Pricing from $199/month/location for up to three providers, dropping to $149/month after twelve months
- True data ownership with anytime export and no vendor lock-in
- eServices including patient portal, payments, web forms, scheduling, secure email, and integrated texting
- Wide third-party integration network through an extensive bridge library

Good for: Cost-conscious practices wanting data ownership without enterprise pricing.

Limitation: Primarily on-premise. Cloud hosting lags behind cloud-native options like Curve.

## Curve Dental

Curve is a fast-growing cloud-based dental practice management system running as a true all-in-one with scheduling, charting, billing, imaging, and patient engagement under one roof.

### What they offer

- No servers or IT overhead, with mobile access via Curve Mobile, HIPAA-compliant AWS encryption, automated backups, and zero-downtime updates
- Configurable invoices, click-to-pay statements, simplified payment posting, and eClaims submission and tracking
- AI-ready data structure powering clinical diagnostics and business analytics

Good for: Growth-focused practices and multi-location groups wanting cloud-native architecture without on-premise infrastructure.

Limitation: Insurance estimates can be inaccurate, forcing staff to revert to manual verification.

## Denticon

Denticon is cloud-based dental practice management software built for multi-location groups. Owned by Planet DDS and, according to the company, used in over 10,000 North American practices, it's positioned as a leading cloud PMS for growth-stage organizations.

### What they offer

- Organization-wide visibility across practices, clinicians, and patients for centralized control
- Treatment planning, native imaging, ortho modules, and voice-activated perio charting
- Multi-location scheduling with patient self-scheduling and family block bookings

Dental revenue cycle management is just the fancy term for not leaving money on the table, and whether you automate it with software or outsource it to a billing service determines how quickly you catch the leaks.

## What Is Dental Revenue Cycle Management?

Dental revenue cycle management (RCM) covers every financial step tied to a patient visit, from booking through final payment.

It pulls together eligibility checks, coding, claims submission, EOB posting, denial work, patient statements, and reconciliation against bank deposits. For an independent practice, the cycle usually looks like this:

- Insurance verification before the appointment
- Treatment planning and accurate procedure coding
- Claims submission to the payer
- EOB retrieval and posting into the PMS
- Reconciliation against bank deposits
- Appeals on denied or underpaid claims
- Patient billing for remaining balances

Each handoff is where money leaks. General medical billing tools rarely map to dental PMS workflows like Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental. What remained were solutions that a solo or small group practice could realistically evaluate and adopt without an enterprise procurement process.

Each vendor was then scored against the five criteria below using only public information: product documentation, pricing pages, PMS integration specs, and published case studies or reviews. No demos were requested, no vendor briefings were held. Where vendor claims could not be corroborated by independent sources, they were noted as unverified rather than taken at face value.

- Automation depth: pure software versus offshore or domestic staffing wrapped in a dashboard
- PMS coverage: full support for Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental, not a single integration

# How Steijn Pelle built Lassie to help small businesses run themselves using AI

### 800+ small businesses across the country are using Lassie to run themselves, and Steijn just raised another $35M to take Lassie to the next level

Katie Kirsch and Cola Gahm

Aug 24, 2026

13

1

2

Share

AI is getting rapidly adopted by Fortune 500 companies and law firms… but what about the millions of small businesses that keep the world running, like your local doctor, plumber, or auto-mechanic?

It turns out, small businesses are more eager to adopt AI than you might think. In fact, hundreds of businesses across the US are now already partly running themselves using AI - including managing paperwork, updating their systems, and soon, interacting and transacting with customers - thanks to Lassie.

Lassie is building the autonomous systems that take care of all the busywork behind running a small business - so that owners can finally focus on what they do best (their craft) and get their time back.

Since founding the company a few years ago, Steijn Pelle has scaled Lassie to 800+ small businesses across 49 states, starting with doctors’ offices. A few months ago, he raised a $35M Series A led by a16z, bringing the company’s total funding to $47M. Now, he’s on a mission to scale Lassie - and create a future world where every small business runs itself, using AI.

---

steijnpelle@steijnpelleToday, we're introducing Lassie and $47M in funding led by a16z. We're building AI that runs small businesses, starting with doctors' offices. Lassie is already trusted by 700+ practices across the country, working autonomously to provide them with 30 hours of labor per month. 2:49 PM · Jun 3, 2026 · 1.19M Views203 Replies · 151 Reposts · 2.91K Likes

---

### The founding story

Before founding Lassie, Steijn was one of the first product managers at both Robinhood and Coinbase - and always had a passion for solving hard problems with technology.

The idea for Lassie came out of a conversation he had with his own doctor, Dr. Kwon, in Menlo Park, CA. Dr. Kwon shared with Steijn that the most challenging part of running his own business wasn’t the craft - it was the 200+ hours per month that he and his team spent on paperwork.

All the tedious, manual, detail-oriented work that they struggled to find staff members to do, and that Dr. Kwon was forced to do himself after-hours - like managing insurance payments, catching underpaid claims, appealing denials, and going back and forth with patients on bills and appointments.

Steijn could sense that there was a huge business opportunity here. Millions of small businesses each spend tens (if not hundreds) of thousands of dollars per year on the kind of busywork that Dr. Kwon was describing.

From left to right: Frédéric Renken, Dr. Kwon, and Steijn Pelle

Steijn also knew it could take years of unglamorous work to fully understand the busywork required to run small businesses - let alone, build a solution that would autonomously run it for business owners in a way that complied with a complex, manual, and highly-regulated industry.

Most founders would have looked right past this space (what Paul Graham calls, “ schlep blindness”) or given up. But for that rare founder with the patience and grit to figure things out from first principles - the reward would be enormous.

This was an opportunity to capture an underserved market that was desperate for a solution to automate the thousands of uninteresting, overlooked tasks that bottleneck small businesses every single day, on a recurring basis.

“AI that autonomously runs small businesses” is what Lassie’s new board member Alex Rampell would call a“Goldilocks zone” - a market that’s not the main priority for frontier AI labs to own themselves, and too messy for a generic model to serve, but big enough to matter.

Maybe it was the competitive runner in him - or that he had seen enough close friends train for years and compete in the Olympics - but Steijn wasn’t afraid of playing the long game. In fact, it was exactly the challenge he had been looking for.

---

### Bringing Lassie to life

You have to learn how to walk before you can run. For Steijn and his team, that meant - you have to learn how to run a small business yourself, before you can train AI to do it for you. So, Steijn and his team signed up to take on all the paperwork for two different doctors’ offices - Dr. Kwon’s in Menlo Park, and a gastroenterologist’s in Scranton. And they didn’t just do this for a few days, then quit - they did this manual work for a year.

To give an example day in the life, Steijn would comb through hundreds of payments from an insurance portal, enter them into the practice management system one by one, print a forty-page list of patients who needed a bill, and finish the day checking everyone’s balances and generating statements. Steijn smiles while thinking about those days: “I felt like Jim Halpert from The Office!”

Co-founders Frédéric Renken (left) and Steijn Pelle (right)

After he and his team figured out the jobs to be done, they started training autonomous systems to do the work for them. Given that they were operating in such a hands-on, heavily-regulated space, handling sensitive financial and personal health information (PHI) - there was no room for error. Lassie didn’t just have to be good, it had to be correct. It took several more years for the product to be ready to scale.

One of the things that had impressed Steijn most at Robinhood was how relentlessly the team worked to seamlessly onboard new users - with little to no manual account approval. Similarly at Superhuman, where his co-founder Frédéric Renken was the first product hire, the team had obsessed over removing friction at the critical moment when people first touch the product.

To learn how to sell and deploy AI at scale, Steijn and his team started by taking the non-scalable approach: first, doing it all in-person. They spent more than a year traveling around the country to visit small business owners, sit with them at their computers, and personally install Lassie onto their systems. Through this, Steijn and his team built a winning playbook for codifying the sale and productizing the implementation of Lassie at scale. Along the way, they also converted their first 100 earliest adopters into some of the biggest champions for the company.

Dr. Kwon is one of those proud early adopters of Lassie - now able to see almost twice as many patients and still make it home in time for dinner with his family. Many customers like him are clinking champagne to celebrate the time Lassie is saving them. Someone recently told Steijn that Lassie “saved his marriage.”

---

### Building the culture and team that scales

A lot has changed since Steijn’s earliest days of building Lassie, but some things haven’t. His approach to operating at the lowest level of detail first, doing things with rigor of thought, and valuing the craft of building something wonderful- is clearly deeply rooted into the company’s culture.

The team is all in. 15 people, in-person in San Francisco, sprinting to make Lassie the AI company that makes entrepreneurship easier for all small businesses. In their first 90 days at the company, every new team member spends time working in a few real small businesses, just like Steijn and Frédéric once did - so they know what it’s like to schlep (err, step) in small business owners’ shoes.

When asked about the most important team values at Lassie, Steijn is quick to answer - the Lassie team doesn’t ship junk, likes rigor of thought, and cares about direct communication.

Steijn is planning to triple the Lassie team in the next year - and he’s about to open a brand-new office in Jackson Square, complete with an open kitchen, beautiful Scandinavian-style co-working spaces, and an in-house chef who previously worked for the Collison brothers.

A glimpse into Lassie’s new San Francisco office

Ultimately, Steijn is in this for the long haul - a marathon of sprints, if you will - and he’s looking for people who are just as persistent and passionate about solving hard problems. If that sounds like you, come build Lassie with him.

---

### Open Roles

Lassie is hiring across the board. A few open roles that stand out:

Deployment Strategist- Be on the frontlines of getting AI deployed to small businesses. And with that build the playbooks for implementation, account management, and maintain the bar for turning customers into fans. Together with the people that did this for Superhuman and Robinhood.

Head of Marketing- Build Lassie’s growth marketing engine that helps to make millions of small business owners aware that AI can now help them run their business.

Product Engineer- Build the products small businesses use every day to get work done without adding more work to manage.

Head of Finance- As Lassie’s first finance hire, you’ll build the AI-native financial operations from scratch alongside CEO Steijn Pelle and advisor Jason Warnick (former CFO, Robinhood) - owning everything from monthly close, strategic finance projects like pricing, and building the operating model, to supporting future fundraises.

Lassie, the company building AI-powered autonomous systems to run small businesses, announced its $35 million Series A financing, bringing its total capital raised to $47 million.

The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) with support from Night Capital, Rahul Vohra (founder and former CEO of Superhuman), Zach Perret (co-founder and CEO of Plaid), Taavet Hinrikus (co-founder and former CEO of Wise), Gokul Rajaram and Brian Balfour.

Orrick represents Lassie.

Lassie helps small businesses run themselves. By pushing the boundaries of autonomous systems, it handles the busywork for business owners. First, doctor’s offices.

Lassie was founded by Steijn Pelle, an early product manager at Robinhood and Coinbase, and Frédéric Renken, the first product hire of Superhuman. It is backed by Andreessen Horowitz, SV Angel, Homebrew, Go Global Ventures, Night Capital, and more. The company currently serves 700+ small businesses, providing owners with over 250,000 hours of labor each year.

"Small business owners should be freed up from doing busywork, so they can focus on what they are passionate about," said Steijn Pelle, CEO and co-founder of Lassie. "After watching 700 businesses rely on Lassie to do a big part of their administration, I am convinced that the future is bright. SAN FRANCISCO, Calif., June 03, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Lassie, the company building autonomous systems to run small businesses, announced it has raised $35 million in Series A financing, bringing its total capital raised to $47 million. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) with support from Night Capital, Rahul Vohra, founder and former CEO of Superhuman; Zach Perret, co-founder and CEO of Plaid; Taavet Hinrikus, co-founder and former CEO of Wise; Gokul Rajaram; and Brian Balfour, co-founder and CEO of Reforge.

AI can do a lot today. It writes software, passes bar exams, and generates realistic videos from simple prompts. But it can do so much more. It can help millions of small business owners by handling their busywork. Up until now, software has not removed this painstaking administrative work and has merely rearranged it. For the first time, software can interpret messy context, move across the endless systems that small businesses have, and do that work for an owner.

Nowhere is this more apparent than in doctors' offices, the largest type of small businesses behind retail and food and beverage. A typical practice loses 100+ hours a month to administrative work and spends roughly $200,000 a year on staff that owners can barely find, let alone keep.

Today, Lassie's agent goes into a practice's insurance portals, pulls reimbursements, reconciles them against records, updates the system-of-record, and verifies the funds in the bank. Operating in more than 700 practices across 49 states, Lassie currently provides businesses owners with over 250,000 hours of labor each year.

"Small business owners should be freed up from doing busywork, so they can focus on what they are passionate about," said Steijn Pelle, CEO and co-founder of Lassie. "After watching 700 businesses rely on Lassie to do a big part of their administration, I am convinced that the future is bright. They now use the time we save them to grow the business and spend more time with customers. And we are just getting started!"

"I am thrilled to partner with Steijn, Frédéric, and the team as they build towards one of the most important shifts in software: from tools that help businesses operate to agents that do the work," said Alex Rampell, co-founder of Affirm and General Partner at a16z. "We think businesses will soon run themselves and Lassie is the perfect example that this is not a pipe dream. They are already making this a reality, providing many businesses with tens of hours of labor each month, and allowing business owners to focus on what they love doing, not busywork."

"Now, Lassie saves us over 100 hours a month and payments that used to take four to five weeks hit our account in less than a week. Most importantly, Lassie has given me time back to focus on my patients, grow my practice, and spend time with my family."

To accelerate Lassie's growth and adoption, the company announced Alex Rampell, co-founder of Affirm and general partner of Andreessen Horowitz, will be joining Lassie's Board of Directors. In addition, Dr. Ed Zuckerberg and Jason Warnick, former chief financial officer of Robinhood, will be joining the company as advisors.

Dental Payment Posting Guide (June 2026)

Your biller sits down with a stack of EOBs, opens Dentrix or Eaglesoft, and keys in payments until the deposit balances. It's the same dental payment posting process most independent practices follow, and it quietly eats 15 to 20 hours every week. The steps themselves are simple: match the claim, post the payment, apply the adjustment, balance the deposit. String them together correctly and posting stops backing up your AR.

TLDR:

- Dental payment posting records insurance and patient payments in your PMS after claims adjudicate.
- Manual posting consumes 80 to 100 hours per month at a typical independent practice.
- Line-by-line posting catches underpayments that lump-sum totals hide, protecting 4 to 7% revenue.
- At least 15% of dental claims are denied on first submission, visible only through EOB review.
- Lassie automates posting across Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental with AI-driven ERA parsing.

## What Is Dental Payment Posting and Why It Matters

Dental payment posting is the day-to-day work of recording insurance and patient payments into your practice management system after claims have been adjudicated. Every check, EFT, virtual card, and patient copay has to land against the right procedure, on the right ledger, with the right adjustment applied. When posting runs cleanly, your AR report tells the truth. When it doesn't, small mismatches compound into weeks of untangling.

A few reasons accurate posting carries weight in an independent practice:

- Cash flow visibility depends on knowing what was actually paid versus what was contractually owed.
- Underpayments, downgrades, and bundling errors only surface if someone matches EOB line items against fee schedules.
- Patient balances cannot be billed correctly until insurance has posted and write-offs are applied.
- Bank reconciliation falls apart when deposits don't tie back to posted payments.

Posting is where revenue gets captured or quietly leaks out.

## The Step-by-Step Dental Payment Posting Process

Here is the workflow most independent practices follow, from the moment a payer remits to the moment the books balance:

1. Receive the remittance. EOBs arrive as paper, faxes, payer portal PDFs, or 835 ERA files. Sort by payer and date of service first.
2. Match to the submitted claim. Confirm procedure codes, dates, and provider on the EOB match what was billed. Discrepancies signal a downgrade or bundling.
3. Post insurance payments line by line. Enter the allowed amount, paid amount, deductible, and coinsurance against each procedure. Lump-sum posting hides errors.
4. Apply contractual adjustments and write-offs. For in-network claims, the gap between billed fee and allowed amount becomes a write-off.
5. Calculate patient responsibility based on remaining balance after credits and copays collected.
6. Balance against the bank deposit. Total posted payments and confirm they match the EFT or check hitting the bank.
7. Flag exceptions for follow-up. Underpayments, denials, and unexpected adjustments go into an appeals worklist, never the closed pile.

## Understanding EOBs and ERAs in Payment Posting

An EOB is the paper or PDF document a payer sends to explain how a claim was adjudicated. An ERA, also called an 835 file, is the electronic version structured for automated import.

Whichever format hits your desk, the line items you need to read are the same:

| Field | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Patient and subscriber | Who the claim belongs to |
| Procedure code (CDT) | What was billed |

## Common Payment Posting Errors and How to Avoid Them

Manual posting is forgiving right up until it isn't. A single misapplied payment can sit on the wrong ledger for months before a patient calls about a mismatched statement. Industry coverage consistently points to delayed or rejected claims as a leading source of lost revenue for dental practices.

The errors that keep showing up:

- Posting to the wrong patient or guarantor, common when family members share a subscriber ID.
- Lump-sum posting against a bulk check, hiding line-level underpayments behind a tidy total.
- Miscalculated write-offs: posting billed minus paid as the adjustment, instead of billed minus allowed.
- Missing payer underpayments when allowed amounts aren't compared to your contracted fee schedule.
- Skipped bank reconciliation, so posted payments and actual deposits drift apart.
- Backlogged posting, where EOBs sitting in a pile turn into aging AR that looks like a collections problem but is actually data entry.

The fix is structural: post line by line, balance to the deposit daily, and route any line that doesn't match the fee schedule into a review queue instead of forcing it through.

## Manual vs. Automated Payment Posting

Most independent practices still post payments by hand. The day looks like this:

- Log into Aetna, Cigna, Delta, MetLife, and a half dozen payer portals.
- Download PDF EOBs from each one.
- Key each line into Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental.
- Tie the day's posts back to the bank deposit.

It works. It also consumes 80 to 100 hours a month at a typical practice.

Automated posting collapses that loop. ERAs and portal EOBs are retrieved on a schedule, parsed against your fee schedule, and written directly to the PMS ledger. A human only touches exceptions.

| Step | Manual | Automated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EOB retrieval | Log into each portal, download | Pulled on schedule |
| Data entry | Keyed line by line | Written to the ledger |
| Write-offs | Calculated per claim | Applied from contracted rates |
| Bank reconciliation | Tallied at day's end | Matched in realtime |
| Exception handling | Mixed into the pile | Routed to a review queue |

The trade-off is real. Automation requires upfront rules configuration and trust in software with money movement. Manual posting requires staff hours that compound every month claim volume grows.

## Key Metrics to Track for Payment Posting Performance

Posting performance is invisible without numbers attached to it. These are the metrics worth pulling monthly:

- Days in AR: average days from claim submission to payment posting. Under 30 is healthy; over 45 signals upstream breakdowns.
- Clean claim rate: percentage of claims paid on first submission without edits. Below 90% points to coding or eligibility gaps.
- Posting turnaround: hours between EOB arrival and ledger entry. Same-day is the target.
- Denial rate: percentage of line items denied per remittance batch.
- Underpayment identification rate: share of paid lines flagged against contracted fee schedules.

Tracked together, these reveal whether posting is keeping pace with collections or quietly falling behind.

## Denial Management and Payment Posting

Posting is where denials become visible. Walking an EOB line by line surfaces every zero-paid procedure with a CARC code attached. Skip that read and denials get buried under the lump-sum total. At least 15% of dental claims are denied on first submission, making denial visibility during posting a revenue protection function.

Common denial reasons surfaced at posting:

- Missing documentation: no narrative, perio chart, or pre-op X-ray attached.
- Coding errors: wrong CDT code, missing tooth number, incorrect surface designation.
- Non-covered service: frequency limit hit, age limit exceeded, or plan exclusion.
- Downgrades posted as denials: composite paid at amalgam rate with the difference miscategorized.
- COB issues: secondary payer denying because the primary EOB wasn't attached.

Accurate CARC/RARC capture creates the audit trail appeals depend on.

Dental Insurance Specialist: What They Do (June 2026)

If your practice is running smoothly until the moment someone asks about a pre-auth, a downgrade, or why their crown wasn't covered the way the front desk promised, you've already felt the gap. Dental insurance coordination falls into a weird zone where it's too detailed for the front desk to handle between appointments but not quite big enough to warrant a full hire until suddenly it is.

Whether you're a practice owner scanning dental insurance specialist jobs near Texas or California to write a job description, a candidate wondering how to become a dental insurance specialist and what the training looks like, or an office manager trying to decide between hiring a dental insurance verification specialist remote or keeping it in-house, the answer depends on volume, complexity, and whether your current team can actually keep up.

Let's break down what a dental insurance specialist does all day, what dental insurance coordinator salaries and hourly pay look like across different setups, and when the role stops being optional and starts paying for itself in recovered revenue.

TLDR:

- Dental insurance specialists verify coverage, submit claims, post EOBs, and handle appeals to get dental practices paid correctly.
- Average salary is $57,372 per year, ranging from $38,500 to $90,000 depending on location and experience.
- You need CDT coding knowledge, PMS experience, and prior dental office work; no degree required.
- Practices with 250+ claims per month or aging AR over 15% should hire a dedicated specialist.
- Lassie automates EOB posting and payment reconciliation, reducing 80–100 monthly admin hours spent reconciling insurance payments by hand.

## What Does a Dental Insurance Specialist Actually Do?

A dental insurance specialist sits between the practice, the patient, and the payer. The job is to ensure claims are paid correctly, on time, and with minimal back-and-forth.

Day to day, the work usually includes:

- Verifying patient eligibility and benefits before appointments
- Pre-authorizing procedures with carriers like Delta Dental, Aetna, Cigna, MetLife, and Guardian
- Submitting clean claims through Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental
- Posting EOBs and payments line by line, applying contracted write-offs and adjustments with Lassie AI
- Matching deposits against bank statements
- Working on aging reports and resubmitting denied or underpaid claims
- Drafting appeals with narratives, X-rays, and chart notes
- Answering patient questions about coverage and balances

One wrong CDT code or missed downgrade can hold up a claim for weeks.

## Dental Insurance Specialist vs. Coordinator vs. Billing Specialist: What's the Difference?

Titles in this corner of the dental world get used interchangeably, creating confusion for job seekers and practice owners writing job descriptions. The roles overlap, but they aren't identical.

| Role | Primary focus | Typical scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insurance coordinator | Patient-facing benefits and treatment plans | Verifies eligibility, explains coverage, and collects estimates |
| Billing specialist | Money in and money out | Submits claims, posts payments, and manages statements |
| Verification specialist | Pre-visit eligibility checks | Confirms coverage, frequencies, downgrades, and waiting periods |
| Insurance specialist | Full insurance lifecycle | Verification, billing, posting, and appeals |

In smaller practices, one person wears every hat. In DSOs, work is split across teams.

## How Much Do Dental Insurance Specialists Make?

Pay varies by location, remote status, and the depth of the revenue cycle your role covers.

Per ZipRecruiter's salary data(as of June 2026), the average dental insurance specialist in the US earns $57,372 per year, with the 25th percentile at $38,500, the 75th percentile at $74,000, and top earners reaching around $90,000 annually.

Geography matters. State-by-state breakdowns put Washington at the top, with New York beating the national average by 9.4%. Texas and California sit mid-pack, though metros like LA, San Francisco, Houston, and Dallas skew higher due to cost of living and DSO density.

Remote roles often pay slightly less than in-office positions in high-cost cities, but offer flexibility and a wider employer pool.

## What Skills and Qualifications Do You Need to Become a Dental Insurance Specialist?

Most employers start with a baseline: a high school diploma or GED, plus a few years in a clerical or front-desk role. A degree isn't required, but ZipRecruiter's role overview notes that prior dental office experience distinguishes entry-level applicants from those who are hireable.

Beyond the basics, hiring managers look for:

- Working knowledge of CDT codes, ICD-10, and common payer policies
- Hands-on experience with Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental
- Comfort reading EOBs, fee schedules, and contracted write-offs
- Phone presence for calling payers and explaining balances to patients
- Attention to detail, since one transposed code can stall a claim

Bilingual candidates, especially Spanish speakers, tend to move faster through the pipeline.

## How to Become a Dental Insurance Specialist: Training and Certification Paths

Most people fall into this role sideways. They start at the front desk, get handed a stack of EOBs, and learn by doing. On-the-job training remains the dominant approach, especially in single-location practices where the office manager mentors directly.

If you want a credential, four programs are worth your time:

- AADOM offers the FAADOM fellowship and insurance-focused coursework
- Dental Career Academy runs a Certified Dental Insurance Specialist program covering CDT coding, claims, and appeals
- Practicon and DentalCodeology publish coding workbooks updated annually for ADA code changes
- Udemy, Coursera, and LinkedIn Learning host shorter billing primers

Pair coursework with hands-on PMS time. Employers care more about claims you've actually worked than certificates on a wall.

## Dental Insurance Specialist Jobs: In-Office, Remote, and Hybrid Opportunities

Remote postings have grown sharply since 2020. Carriers like MCNA Dental, Delta Dental, and Guardian routinely list work-from-home triage and CSR roles, while DSOs centralize billing teams in regional hubs serving dozens of locations.

What each setup typically looks like:

- In-office: $18 to $24 per hour, full PMS access, direct patient contact
- Hybrid: $20 to $27 per hour, two or three days on-site, common at multi-location practices
- Fully remote: $21 to $30 per hour, requires a HIPAA-compliant workspace, secure VPN, and usually two-plus years of prior in-office experience

Remote roles favor candidates who self-manage and document everything.

## When Does a Dental Practice Actually Need a Dedicated Insurance Specialist?

There's no universal threshold, but four signals usually mean it's time to dedicate someone to insurance work full-time.

Consider hiring when you hit any of these:

- More than 250 claims per month (a widely used industry rule of thumb, or two-plus providers producing steadily
- Aging over 90 days creeping past 15% of total AR, is a widely cited benchmark in dental revenue cycle management
- Front desk staff are missing eligibility checks or skipping appeals to keep the schedule moving
- Insurance write-offs exceeding what your office manager can audit weekly

The math is simple. If a $55K specialist recovers an extra $80K in written-off claims and frees your front desk to book more treatment, the role pays for itself before year one closes.

## In-House Insurance Specialist vs. Outsourcing to a Billing Company: Weighing Your Options

Once volume warrants dedicated insurance work, the next call is whether to hire or hand it off.

In-house wins when patient relationships drive collections and the front desk needs someone on-site. Outsourcing to a billing agency fits when claim volume swings unpredictably, turnover keeps gutting your billing seat, or you'd rather skip managing another W-2 employee. A third path is software-first automation: Lassie handles EOB posting, payment matching, and secondary claim filing without a human biller doing the work. It sits between the two — lower overhead than a full-service agency, higher accuracy than a rotating staff seat — and leaves your specialist free to work appeals, verifications, and patient-facing questions instead of keying line items.

Even seasoned specialists hit the same walls. The fix is usually a tighter process, not more hours.

- Denials and rejections: build a denial log by reason code, then attack the top three causes monthly instead of appealing one by one
- Shifting payer policies: subscribe to Delta Dental, Cigna, and MetLife provider bulletins, and assign one team member to summarize updates weekly
- Verification crunch: batch verifications 72 hours out using payer portals, reserving live calls for exceptions
- Coordination of benefits: document birthday rule and primary/secondary logic in a one-page workstation reference
- Difficult carrier reps: get a reference number on every call and escalate in writing when answers contradict the contract

How Steijn Pelle built Lassie to help small businesses run themselves using AI

Agree & Join LinkedIn

By clicking Continue to join or sign in, you agree to LinkedIn’s User Agreement, Privacy Policy, and Cookie Policy.

AI is getting rapidly adopted by Fortune 500 companies and law firms… but what about the millions of small businesses that keep the world running, like your local doctor, plumber, or auto-mechanic?

It turns out, small businesses are more eager to adopt AI than you might think. In fact, hundreds of businesses across the US are now already partly running themselves using AI - including managing paperwork, updating their systems, and soon, interacting and transacting with customers - thanks to Lassie.

Lassie is building the autonomous systems that take care of all the busywork behind running a small business - so that owners can finally focus on what they do best (their craft) and get their time back.

Since founding the company a few years ago, Steijn Pelle has scaled Lassie to 800+ small businesses across 49 states, starting with doctors’ offices. A few months ago, he raised a $35M Series A led by a16z, bringing the company’s total funding to $47M. Now, he’s on a mission to scale Lassie - and create a future world where every small business runs itself, using AI.

---

### The founding story

Before founding Lassie, Steijn was one of the first product managers at both Robinhood and Coinbase - and always had a passion for solving hard problems with technology.

The idea for Lassie came out of a conversation he had with his own doctor, Dr. Kwon, in Menlo Park, CA. Dr. Kwon shared with Steijn that the most challenging part of running his own business wasn’t the craft - it was the 200+ hours per month that he and his team spent on paperwork.

All the tedious, manual, detail-oriented work that they struggled to find staff members to do, and that Dr. Kwon was forced to do himself after-hours - like managing insurance payments, catching underpaid claims, appealing denials, and going back and forth with patients on bills and appointments.

Steijn could sense that there was a huge business opportunity here. Millions of small businesses each spend tens (if not hundreds) of thousands of dollars per year on the kind of busywork that Dr. Kwon was describing.

From left to right: Frédéric Renken, Dr. Kwon, and Steijn Pelle

Steijn also knew it could take years of unglamorous work to fully understand the busywork required to run small businesses - let alone, build a solution that would autonomously run it for business owners in a way that complied with a complex, manual, and highly-regulated industry.

99% of founders would have looked right past this space (what Paul Graham calls, “ schlep blindness”) or given up. But for that rare founder with the patience and grit to figure things out from first principles - the reward would be enormous.

This was an opportunity to capture an underserved market that was desperate for a solution to automate the thousands of uninteresting, overlooked tasks that bottleneck small businesses every single day, on a recurring basis.

“AI that autonomously runs small businesses” is what Lassie’s new board member Alex Rampell would call a“Goldilocks zone” - a market that’s not the main priority for frontier AI labs to own themselves, and too messy for a generic model to serve, but big enough to matter.

Maybe it was the competitive runner in him - or that he had seen enough close friends train for years and compete in the Olympics - but Steijn wasn’t afraid of playing the long game. In fact, it was exactly the challenge he had been looking for.

---

### Bringing Lassie to life

You have to learn how to walk before you can run. For Steijn and his team, that meant - you have to learn how to run a small business yourself, before you can train AI to do it for you. So, Steijn and his team signed up to take on all the paperwork for two different doctors’ offices - Dr. Kwon’s in Menlo Park, and a gastroenterologist’s in Scranton. And they didn’t just do this for a few days, then quit - they did this manual work for a year.

To give an example day in the life, Steijn would comb through hundreds of payments from an insurance portal, enter them into the practice management system one by one, print a forty-page list of patients who needed a bill, and finish the day checking everyone’s balances and generating statements. Steijn smiles while thinking about those days: “I felt like Jim Halpert from The Office!”

Co-founders Frédéric Renken (left) and Steijn Pelle (right)

After he and his team figured out the jobs to be done, they started training autonomous systems to do the work for them. Given that they were operating in such a hands-on, heavily-regulated space, handling sensitive financial and personal health information (PHI) - there was no room for error. Lassie didn’t just have to be good, it had to be correct. It took several more years for the product to be ready to scale.

One of the things that had impressed Steijn most at Robinhood was how relentlessly the team worked to seamlessly onboard new users - with little to no manual account approval. Similarly at Superhuman, where his co-founder Frédéric Renken was the first product hire, the team had obsessed over removing friction at the critical moment when people first touch the product.

To learn how to sell and deploy AI at scale, Steijn and his team started by taking the non-scalable approach: first, doing it all in-person. They spent more than a year traveling around the country to visit small business owners, sit with them at their computers, and personally install Lassie onto their systems. Through this, Steijn and his team built a winning playbook for codifying the sale and productizing the implementation of Lassie at scale. Along the way, they also converted their first 100 earliest adopters into some of the biggest champions for the company.

Dr. Kwon is one of those proud early adopters of Lassie - now able to see almost twice as many patients and still make it home in time for dinner with his family. Many customers like him are clinking champagne to celebrate how much time Lassie is saving them. Someone recently told Steijn that Lassie “saved his marriage.”

---

### Building the culture and team that scales

A lot has changed since Steijn’s earliest days of building Lassie, but some things haven’t. His approach to operating at the lowest level of detail first, doing things with rigor of thought, and valuing the craft of building something wonderful- is clearly deeply rooted into the company’s culture.

The team is all in. 15 people, in-person in San Francisco, sprinting to make Lassie the AI company that makes entrepreneurship easier for all small businesses. In their first 90 days at the company, every new team member spends time working in a few real small businesses, just like Steijn and Frédéric once did - so they know what it’s like to schlep (err, step) in small business owners’ shoes.

When asked about the most important team values at Lassie, Steijn is quick to answer - the Lassie team doesn’t ship junk, likes rigor of thought, and cares about direct communication.

Steijn is planning to triple the Lassie team in the next year - and he’s about to open a brand-new office in Jackson Square, complete with an open kitchen, beautiful Scandinavian-style co-working spaces, and an in-house chef who previously worked for the Collison brothers.

A glimpse into Lassie’s new San Francisco office

Ultimately, Steijn is in this for the long haul - a marathon of sprints, if you will - and he’s looking for people who are just as persistent and passionate about solving hard problems. If that sounds like you, come build Lassie with him.

---

### Open Roles

Lassie is hiring across the board. A few open roles that stand out:

- Deployment Strategist- Be on the frontlines of getting AI deployed to small businesses. And with that build the playbooks for implementation, account management, and maintain the bar for turning customers into fans. Together with the people that did this for Superhuman and Robinhood.
- Head of Marketing- Build Lassie’s growth marketing engine that helps to make millions of small business owners aware that AI can now help them run their business.
- Product Engineer- Build the products small businesses use every day to get work done without adding more work to manage.
- Head of Finance- As Lassie’s first finance hire, you’ll build the AI-native financial operations from scratch alongside CEO Steijn Pelle and advisor Jason Warnick (former CFO, Robinhood) - owning everything from monthly close, strategic finance projects like pricing, and building the operating model, to supporting future fundraises.
- Founding Recruiter- Help recruit a world-class team that can bring AI to millions of small businesses across the world.

company for a sales team that sells an AI account-based-marketing platform.

  Domain: www.lassie.ai (the marketing site also resolves at getlassie.com)

  Founders: Steijn Pelle and Frederic (Frederik) Renken. Raised a $35M Series A led by Andreessen
  Horowitz, announced 3 June 2026.

DISAMBIGUATION - THIS IS CRITICAL. Several unrelated entities share the name "Lassie":
  - Lassie (lassie.co / lassie.se), a Swedish/European PET INSURANCE company - NOT the target.
  - Lassie, the fictional collie / the film and TV franchise - NOT the target.
  - Any veterinary, pet-care, or dog-related "Lassie" - NOT the target.
If a source is about pet insurance, pets, dogs, or the TV collie, DISCARD it and say so. Only use
sources that are unambiguously about the SF dental/healthcare-admin AI company at lassie.ai.

Ground EVERY fact in a public page. For every fact give: the fact, a VERBATIM QUOTE copied exactly
from the source, and the SOURCE URL. If a fact cannot be found on a public page, write
"NOT FOUND" - never guess, never infer a number, never fill a gap with a plausible-sounding claim.
Prefer primary sources (lassie.ai pages, the company's own job postings on jobs.ashbyhq.com/lassie,
the a16z announcement, the BusinessWire release, founder posts) over aggregators.

Write a long, dense, well-organised markdown report with these numbered sections. Do not skip a
section; if a section has nothing, write the heading and "NOT FOUND".

1. IDENTITY AND DISAMBIGUATION - legal/operating name, HQ, founding year, what it actually sells,
   in one paragraph; then an explicit list of same-name entities you EXCLUDED and why.
2. PRODUCT AND TARGET VERTICAL - exactly what the product does, which practice types it serves
   (dental? medical? veterinary?), which workflows it automates (claims, EOB, insurance
   verification, phone, scheduling), pricing if public, integrations/PMS or EHR systems named.
   Quote the product pages.
3. CUSTOMERS AND TRACTION - number of practices/dentists served, named customers, ARR or revenue
   claims, growth claims, testimonials. Quote each.
4. FUNDING HISTORY - every round with date, amount, stage, lead investor, participating investors,
   and the announcement URL. Include any seed/pre-seed round before the Series A.
5. TEAM AND GTM COMPOSITION - total headcount, engineering vs sales vs marketing split, and

   employee you can find with their title (LinkedIn, team page, job postings, press).
6. GO-TO-MARKET MOTION - hard evidence of HOW they acquire customers: founder-led selling,

   conferences/trade shows, partnerships with DSOs or dental service organizations. Quote the
   evidence. Also: any public evidence of the sales/marketing TOOLS they use (CRM, outbound
   tooling, ad platforms).
7. HIRING SIGNALS - every open role you can find, especially go-to-market roles (growth, GTM,

   if published.
8. LEADERSHIP AND KEY PEOPLE - the founders and any executives/leads, with exact titles, prior
   companies, and a source URL each. Flag who appears to own revenue/growth.
9. OPERATIONAL PAIN AND STRATEGIC MOVES - what problems the company itself is publicly wrestling
